source.title: Scalable Physics-Inspired Transformers for Spin Glasses
source.authors: Lu Zhong; Wenli Duan; Jing Liu; Pan Zhang; Ying Tang

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary information are present. No apparent truncation or garbling that prevents reading the relevant sections.
record.tranche_reason: The paper contrasts spin-glass autoregressive models with language-model scaling, but does not test the stated power laws for language-model held-out loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its own parameter-count comparison uses spin-glass ground-state residual energy, a different measure and task.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions monotonic scaling in LLMs and says spin-glass VANs have lacked a clear scaling advantage. It does not measure language-model cross-entropy, fit scaling laws in parameters, tokens, or compute, test extrapolation from smaller runs, or evaluate compute-optimal allocations. The supplementary comparison of parameter count and spin-glass residual energy is recorded under fits_no_version; cited results from other studies are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a transformer sampler for spin glasses and only mentions LLM scaling laws as motivation. It measures no pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It fits no power law and tests no extrapolation or compute-optimal split. Its parameter-count comparison (Supp. Fig. 10) uses spin-glass residual energy for a variational sampler. That is a different construct and training regime, and no power-law form is fitted, so V5 is not tested either.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that scalability comes from physics-inspired sparse attention, concatenated positional embeddings, FlashAttention with a KV cache, and a training strategy combining local Monte Carlo refinement with self-distillation. They report up to two orders of magnitude speedup and accurate free energies, ground states and overlap distributions up to 4,096 spins. They make no claim about language-model scaling laws beyond contrasting them with prior spin-glass models.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies autoregressive spin-glass sampling and thermodynamic estimates, not the language-model pretraining-loss measurements or compute-optimal allocation methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: In the spin-glass experiments, performance varies with positional-embedding design and dimension allocation, patching, and training strategy; these are not tests of the claim's language-model scaling laws.

fits_no_version.finding: On 2D EA ground-state search, the MADE sampler does not reach low error at L=32 despite tens of millions of parameters. FlashVAN reaches about 1e-6 relative error at L=8, including with patching. No power-law fit is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For variational autoregressive spin-glass samplers, adding parameters alone does not reliably reduce residual energy; architecture and input compression dominate.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors state that spin-glass autoregressive models show no clear scaling advantage, unlike LLMs. This is a motivating statement, not a measured scaling curve.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scale-driven performance gains seen in language models may not transfer to variational samplers for frustrated spin systems.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says a PyTorch implementation will be publicly available upon acceptance, but gives no URL
record.problems: No held-out language-model loss, model/token/compute scaling fit, extrapolation test, or compute-optimal allocation analysis. The related parameter-count comparison concerns spin-glass residual energy; exact plotted values are not stated in the text. Some reported spin-glass estimates are averaged over five disorder instances.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were omitted. The paper's other model-size, thermodynamic, overlap-distribution, and timing results do not measure the behaviors named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens.
No language-model shape comparison at fixed parameter count. The positional-embedding allocation experiments concern spin samplers, not loss scaling.
No power-law fit of loss with scale for the spin-glass variational models. The finite-size fits are over physical system size, not model scale.
No downstream task performance related to scale or loss.
No exponents or compute-optimal splits refitted.

record.verdict_notes: The 'scaling' in this paper is mostly scaling in physical system size (finite-size corrections) and runtime, not model-scale loss laws. It is correctly classified T6 / discusses.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model loss or parameter, token, or compute scaling law is measured.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger language-model runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens is tested.
The paper does not compare language-model depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count using held-out loss.
The paper studies spin-glass models, but does not test whether the specified held-out-loss power-law form holds in that setting or another modality.
No downstream language task performance is related to pretraining loss or scale.
No language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation are refitted or compared across setup choices.
